cells.tense: You're in the middle of it right now, and your hands are on the scale.
cells.ask: Set one thing that's been out of proportion back to what it should be, today, and let the adjustment be visible to whoever it affects.
cells.core:
You know what's owed and you're not guessing about it. When something's out of line, you feel the distance and you close it — not with a speech but with the actual correction, the thing moved back where it belongs. That's why people bring you the hard split to call.

The proof is already there: a stretched week that got rebalanced because you noticed, a scale that tipped and you put it level without anyone thanking you. What you're free to do next is let a little more of it be seen — let one person hear that the call was yours, said out loud, so the correction and the credit arrive together.
cells.sheetLine: You feel the imbalance and you correct it. That's the whole act.
cells.verb: gathering what was scattered and holding one chosen direction
cells.place: in the part of a life where you weigh what's owed and set things back in proportion

cells.tense: You're already living past the moment, bracing for something that hasn't happened yet.
cells.ask: Pick the one imbalance you're most braced about and write down, on paper, what you'd actually do if it went badly — then leave the page for a day.
cells.core:
You're defending a line nobody is pushing on yet. The gathering has gone past what's needed: you're weighing outcomes before the outcome exists, running the correction in a future that hasn't had a chance to be fair on its own. The care looks like control, and the control is wearing the care thin.

When this is working, you're the one who can hold a complicated split in your head and just see what's level. That's real, and it isn't the same as pre-running every bad version. Coming back to one fact at a time, nothing predicted, hands you back a settled mind — the ground you're currently spending before it arrives.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding your ground against something you can't see yet.
cells.verb: gathering what was scattered and holding one chosen direction

cells.tense: You knew what was owed once, and you're standing where it went quiet.
cells.ask: Pick the one imbalance that still stings and write the sentence you'd have said then — not to send, just to finish it on paper.
cells.core:
The scale goes unread. When it's working, you say the arrangement is off, someone hears it, and it shifts a notch toward level — that plain act is the whole thing, and you've done it before. You stopped calling what's out of proportion, so things set the way they set and you went along with a version of balance that isn't yours. What's missing isn't care.

It's the willingness to say the thing is off and trust that naming it moves toward level rather than making it worse. The part of you that weighs and corrects hasn't gone anywhere. Finish the old sentence and the present one has somewhere to start from.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped calling out what's out of proportion.

cells.tense: The scale is already being read and you're not admitting it was your hand.
cells.ask: Name one arrangement you've been treating as just how things are and say out loud that you set it that way.
cells.core:
When this is working, you know you're the one holding the scale — you decide who gets what, which thing sits level and which gets left tipped — and you say so, and people can come to you about it. The correction is running anyway: you're choosing who gets what, and you've been describing it as the situation.

Somewhere in there the weighing is yours, and calling it nobody's keeps you out of the room where the balance is actually made. That's a real thing to give up: if the fairness was yours to make, it's also yours if it's off. Say the claim once and the next adjustment gets a hand that owns it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep adjusting it and calling it just how things are.
